tools.name: vm_troubleshoot
tools.description: Diagnose KubeVirt VirtualMachine issues with automated root-cause detection. Collects VM status, VMI status, volumes, DataVolume/PVC state, cloud-init configuration, pod state, logs, and events, then runs heuristic checks to identify specific problems and suggest fixes. Returns a 'Detected Issues' section with CRITICAL/WARNING findings and actionable remediation steps, followed by raw diagnostic data. Use this tool FIRST whenever a user asks why a VM is not starting, stuck in Provisioning, crashlooping, failing to migrate, or exhibiting unexpected behavior. Automatically detects: missing StorageClasses, invalid PVC specs, dangerous cloud-init commands (shutdown/halt), nodeSelector migration blockers, failed migrations, and pod crashloops. If the user asks to fix or remediate the issue, use the Suggested Fixes from the report with vm_lifecycle (restart) or resources_create_or_update.

name.description: The name of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

namespace.description: The namespace of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

  - command: ["nginx"]

  - kept image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged

- remove the explicit command/args to use the image’s default entrypoint instead, or
- create a Service/Ingress to expose it?

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

Root cause:
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That kept the PVC Pending and the pod unschedulable.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss because it never bound to a volume).
- Recreated it using the default StorageClass "standard" (rancher.io/local-path).

Current state:
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass "standard".

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch the PVC accordingly. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Fixed.

Root cause:
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That kept the PVC Pending and the pod unschedulable.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss because it never bound to a volume).
- Recreated it using the default StorageClass "standard" (rancher.io/local-path).

Current state:
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass "standard".

- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

Root cause:
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That kept the PVC Pending and the pod unschedulable.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss because it never bound to a volume).
- Recreated it using the default StorageClass "standard" (rancher.io/local-path).

Current state:
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass "standard".

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch the PVC accordingly. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but:
  - Liveness/Readiness probes were checking http://:80/get_status and /is_ready (wrong port and paths).
  - The Service targeted container port 80 (no listener there).
- Result: probes failed and the app was not becoming Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: webapp-b8996969f-7f96f is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service: webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.227.21) points to the pod on port 8080.
- Endpoints are healthy (10.244.0.49:8080).

How to access it
- In-cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your workstation: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress to expose it outside the cluster—tell me the hostname you want to use.

Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but:
  - Liveness/Readiness probes were checking http://:80/get_status and /is_ready (wrong port and paths).
  - The Service targeted container port 80 (no listener there).
- Result: probes failed and the app was not becoming Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: webapp-b8996969f-7f96f is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service: webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.227.21) points to the pod on port 8080.
- Endpoints are healthy (10.244.0.49:8080).

How to access it
- In-cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your workstation: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress to expose it outside the cluster—tell me the hostname you want to use.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but:
  - Liveness/Readiness probes were checking http://:80/get_status and /is_ready (wrong port and paths).
  - The Service targeted container port 80 (no listener there).
- Result: probes failed and the app was not becoming Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: webapp-b8996969f-7f96f is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service: webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.227.21) points to the pod on port 8080.
- Endpoints are healthy (10.244.0.49:8080).

How to access it
- In-cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your workstation: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 then open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress to expose it outside the cluster—tell me the hostname you want to use.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant permissions on pods (core API group). So the pod-reader ServiceAccount had no right to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include permission to list pods in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept the existing deployments list rule.

Bindings look correct
- RoleBinding pod-reader-binding correctly binds simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to Role/pod-reader-role in the same namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you also want to get individual pods or watch them, I can add get and watch verbs too—just say the word.

  namespace: simple-rbac-setup

  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["list"]

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant permissions on pods (core API group). So the pod-reader ServiceAccount had no right to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include permission to list pods in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept the existing deployments list rule.

Bindings look correct
- RoleBinding pod-reader-binding correctly binds simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to Role/pod-reader-role in the same namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you also want to get individual pods or watch them, I can add get and watch verbs too—just say the word.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant permissions on pods (core API group). So the pod-reader ServiceAccount had no right to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include permission to list pods in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept the existing deployments list rule.

Bindings look correct
- RoleBinding pod-reader-binding correctly binds simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to Role/pod-reader-role in the same namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you also want to get individual pods or watch them, I can add get and watch verbs too—just say the word.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web but your Deployment/pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (so it selects the nginx pods)
  - ports.targetPort: 8080 (container’s actual port)
- Result: Endpoints now show the pod at 10.244.0.51:8080 and the Service works.

Verification performed
- From inside the pod, port 80 was closed; port 8080 returned HTTP 200 OK.
- After the fix:
  - Endpoints: nginx → 10.244.0.51:8080
  - Curling the ClusterIP and DNS name returned HTTP 200 OK.

How you can confirm
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- Test from within the cluster (e.g., any pod): curl -I http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local or curl -I http://<ClusterIP>

If you need external access
- There’s no Ingress defined in web and the Service is ClusterIP, so it won’t be reachable from outside the cluster as-is.
- Options:
  1) Switch Service to NodePort (quick): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}' then reach http://<nodeIP>:<allocatedNodePort>
  2) Create an Ingress (preferred behind an Ingress Controller). I can set this up if you tell me the host/path you want.

Let me know if you want me to expose it externally and by which method (NodePort/Ingress/LoadBalancer).

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web but your Deployment/pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (so it selects the nginx pods)
  - ports.targetPort: 8080 (container’s actual port)
- Result: Endpoints now show the pod at 10.244.0.51:8080 and the Service works.

Verification performed
- From inside the pod, port 80 was closed; port 8080 returned HTTP 200 OK.
- After the fix:
  - Endpoints: nginx → 10.244.0.51:8080
  - Curling the ClusterIP and DNS name returned HTTP 200 OK.

How you can confirm
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- Test from within the cluster (e.g., any pod): curl -I http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local or curl -I http://<ClusterIP>

If you need external access
- There’s no Ingress defined in web and the Service is ClusterIP, so it won’t be reachable from outside the cluster as-is.
- Options:
  1) Switch Service to NodePort (quick): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}' then reach http://<nodeIP>:<allocatedNodePort>
  2) Create an Ingress (preferred behind an Ingress Controller). I can set this up if you tell me the host/path you want.

Let me know if you want me to expose it externally and by which method (NodePort/Ingress/LoadBalancer).

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web but your Deployment/pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (so it selects the nginx pods)
  - ports.targetPort: 8080 (container’s actual port)
- Result: Endpoints now show the pod at 10.244.0.51:8080 and the Service works.

Verification performed
- From inside the pod, port 80 was closed; port 8080 returned HTTP 200 OK.
- After the fix:
  - Endpoints: nginx → 10.244.0.51:8080
  - Curling the ClusterIP and DNS name returned HTTP 200 OK.

How you can confirm
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- Test from within the cluster (e.g., any pod): curl -I http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local or curl -I http://<ClusterIP>

If you need external access
- There’s no Ingress defined in web and the Service is ClusterIP, so it won’t be reachable from outside the cluster as-is.
- Options:
  1) Switch Service to NodePort (quick): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}' then reach http://<nodeIP>:<allocatedNodePort>
  2) Create an Ingress (preferred behind an Ingress Controller). I can set this up if you tell me the host/path you want.

Let me know if you want me to expose it externally and by which method (NodePort/Ingress/LoadBalancer).

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector on the Deployment: environment: production-gpu. Your cluster’s node(s) do not have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. This left the Service with no endpoints, causing connection refused when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector”
  - Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu
  - Service Endpoints were empty before the fix

What I changed
- Removed the unsatisfiable nodeSelector from the Deployment (recreated it to fully clear the field).
- Left everything else the same (replicas=2, image=quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest, port 80).

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-l9mrc (10.244.0.53)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-trqkm (10.244.0.54)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.53:80, 10.244.0.54:80
- The Service web-app-service in namespace webshop-frontend now has healthy backends, so connection errors should be resolved.

How you can verify
- Check pods:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -l app=web-app -o wide
- Check service endpoints:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- Test in-cluster connectivity:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service

If you actually need the nodeSelector
- Add the label to an appropriate node, then re-add the selector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
  - I can reapply the selector to the Deployment if you confirm the correct label/target nodes.
- Alternatively, use tolerations/affinity if you’re targeting specific node types.

Optional hardening
- Add readiness/liveness probes to avoid routing to a container before it’s ready (nginx is fast, but this is good practice). I can add these if you’d like.

Let me know if you want me to restore a constrained placement (with the correct label) or tune probes/resources.

Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector on the Deployment: environment: production-gpu. Your cluster’s node(s) do not have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. This left the Service with no endpoints, causing connection refused when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector”
  - Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu
  - Service Endpoints were empty before the fix

What I changed
- Removed the unsatisfiable nodeSelector from the Deployment (recreated it to fully clear the field).
- Left everything else the same (replicas=2, image=quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest, port 80).

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-l9mrc (10.244.0.53)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-trqkm (10.244.0.54)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.53:80, 10.244.0.54:80
- The Service web-app-service in namespace webshop-frontend now has healthy backends, so connection errors should be resolved.

How you can verify
- Check pods:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -l app=web-app -o wide
- Check service endpoints:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- Test in-cluster connectivity:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service

If you actually need the nodeSelector
- Add the label to an appropriate node, then re-add the selector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
  - I can reapply the selector to the Deployment if you confirm the correct label/target nodes.
- Alternatively, use tolerations/affinity if you’re targeting specific node types.

Optional hardening
- Add readiness/liveness probes to avoid routing to a container before it’s ready (nginx is fast, but this is good practice). I can add these if you’d like.

Let me know if you want me to restore a constrained placement (with the correct label) or tune probes/resources.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector on the Deployment: environment: production-gpu. Your cluster’s node(s) do not have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. This left the Service with no endpoints, causing connection refused when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector”
  - Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu
  - Service Endpoints were empty before the fix

What I changed
- Removed the unsatisfiable nodeSelector from the Deployment (recreated it to fully clear the field).
- Left everything else the same (replicas=2, image=quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest, port 80).

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-l9mrc (10.244.0.53)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-trqkm (10.244.0.54)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.53:80, 10.244.0.54:80
- The Service web-app-service in namespace webshop-frontend now has healthy backends, so connection errors should be resolved.

How you can verify
- Check pods:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -l app=web-app -o wide
- Check service endpoints:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- Test in-cluster connectivity:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service

If you actually need the nodeSelector
- Add the label to an appropriate node, then re-add the selector:
  - kubectl label node <your-node> environment=production-gpu
  - I can reapply the selector to the Deployment if you confirm the correct label/target nodes.
- Alternatively, use tolerations/affinity if you’re targeting specific node types.

Optional hardening
- Add readiness/liveness probes to avoid routing to a container before it’s ready (nginx is fast, but this is good practice). I can add these if you’d like.

Let me know if you want me to restore a constrained placement (with the correct label) or tune probes/resources.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the requested multi-tenant dev environment with isolated namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies. Here’s what’s in place.

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer admin to their own namespace:
  - RoleBindings: owner-admin-binding in dev-alice (alice), dev-bob (bob), dev-charlie (charlie) bound to ClusterRole admin
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - Each SA has full access to its own namespace via sa-admin-binding (ClusterRole admin)
- Read-only to shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-users in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to users alice, bob, charlie
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-sas in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to SAs: alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings were created. With RBAC, absence of permissions means only cluster-admins can access.

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

NetworkPolicies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all six namespaces
- Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace (separate allow-same-namespace ingress/egress policies)
- Allow DNS egress in all namespaces (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns/coredns in kube-system)
- Dev namespace egress is restricted to:
  - own namespace
  - dev-shared namespace
  - DNS
- dev-shared allows ingress from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (and itself)
- staging and prod are isolated from dev namespaces (only same-namespace traffic + DNS egress is allowed)

Notes and recommended follow-ups
- Least privilege on RBAC: today, developers and their SAs have “admin” in their own namespaces (per requirement of “full access”). If you prefer “edit” (can’t manage RBAC) instead of “admin,” we can switch by deleting and recreating those RoleBindings (roleRef is immutable). Say the word and I’ll update them to edit.
- Internet egress: current policies intentionally do NOT allow internet egress (only same-namespace, dev->dev-shared, and DNS). If developers need to pull from external APIs/registries at runtime, we can add an allow-egress-to-internet NetworkPolicy (for example with ipBlock 0.0.0.0/0 limited to required ports).
- Kubernetes API access from pods: many workloads call the in-cluster API (kubernetes.default.svc). If you need this, we can add a small egress policy to allow TCP 443 to that service/endpoint (varies by distro).
- Network plugin: these NetworkPolicies require a CNI that implements Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.). If you’re using a basic CNI without policy support, enforcement won’t occur.
- Verify what’s applied:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl get rolebindings -A | egrep 'dev-|staging|prod'
  - kubectl get resourcequota -A
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -A
- Developer ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes v1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa --duration=24h
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa --duration=24h
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa --duration=24h

Want me to:
- switch own-namespace RoleBindings from admin to edit for stricter least privilege?
- enable controlled internet egress for any namespace(s)?
- add an explicit allow to the in-cluster Kubernetes API?

Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the requested multi-tenant dev environment with isolated namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies. Here’s what’s in place.

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer admin to their own namespace:
  - RoleBindings: owner-admin-binding in dev-alice (alice), dev-bob (bob), dev-charlie (charlie) bound to ClusterRole admin
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - Each SA has full access to its own namespace via sa-admin-binding (ClusterRole admin)
- Read-only to shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-users in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to users alice, bob, charlie
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-sas in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to SAs: alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings were created. With RBAC, absence of permissions means only cluster-admins can access.

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

NetworkPolicies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all six namespaces
- Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace (separate allow-same-namespace ingress/egress policies)
- Allow DNS egress in all namespaces (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns/coredns in kube-system)
- Dev namespace egress is restricted to:
  - own namespace
  - dev-shared namespace
  - DNS
- dev-shared allows ingress from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (and itself)
- staging and prod are isolated from dev namespaces (only same-namespace traffic + DNS egress is allowed)

Notes and recommended follow-ups
- Least privilege on RBAC: today, developers and their SAs have “admin” in their own namespaces (per requirement of “full access”). If you prefer “edit” (can’t manage RBAC) instead of “admin,” we can switch by deleting and recreating those RoleBindings (roleRef is immutable). Say the word and I’ll update them to edit.
- Internet egress: current policies intentionally do NOT allow internet egress (only same-namespace, dev->dev-shared, and DNS). If developers need to pull from external APIs/registries at runtime, we can add an allow-egress-to-internet NetworkPolicy (for example with ipBlock 0.0.0.0/0 limited to required ports).
- Kubernetes API access from pods: many workloads call the in-cluster API (kubernetes.default.svc). If you need this, we can add a small egress policy to allow TCP 443 to that service/endpoint (varies by distro).
- Network plugin: these NetworkPolicies require a CNI that implements Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.). If you’re using a basic CNI without policy support, enforcement won’t occur.
- Verify what’s applied:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl get rolebindings -A | egrep 'dev-|staging|prod'
  - kubectl get resourcequota -A
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -A
- Developer ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes v1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa --duration=24h
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa --duration=24h
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa --duration=24h

Want me to:
- switch own-namespace RoleBindings from admin to edit for stricter least privilege?
- enable controlled internet egress for any namespace(s)?
- add an explicit allow to the in-cluster Kubernetes API?

  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created the requested multi-tenant dev environment with isolated namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies. Here’s what’s in place.

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer admin to their own namespace:
  - RoleBindings: owner-admin-binding in dev-alice (alice), dev-bob (bob), dev-charlie (charlie) bound to ClusterRole admin
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
  - Each SA has full access to its own namespace via sa-admin-binding (ClusterRole admin)
- Read-only to shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-users in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to users alice, bob, charlie
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-view-sas in dev-shared grants ClusterRole view to SAs: alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings were created. With RBAC, absence of permissions means only cluster-admins can access.

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

NetworkPolicies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all six namespaces
- Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace (separate allow-same-namespace ingress/egress policies)
- Allow DNS egress in all namespaces (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns/coredns in kube-system)
- Dev namespace egress is restricted to:
  - own namespace
  - dev-shared namespace
  - DNS
- dev-shared allows ingress from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (and itself)
- staging and prod are isolated from dev namespaces (only same-namespace traffic + DNS egress is allowed)

Notes and recommended follow-ups
- Least privilege on RBAC: today, developers and their SAs have “admin” in their own namespaces (per requirement of “full access”). If you prefer “edit” (can’t manage RBAC) instead of “admin,” we can switch by deleting and recreating those RoleBindings (roleRef is immutable). Say the word and I’ll update them to edit.
- Internet egress: current policies intentionally do NOT allow internet egress (only same-namespace, dev->dev-shared, and DNS). If developers need to pull from external APIs/registries at runtime, we can add an allow-egress-to-internet NetworkPolicy (for example with ipBlock 0.0.0.0/0 limited to required ports).
- Kubernetes API access from pods: many workloads call the in-cluster API (kubernetes.default.svc). If you need this, we can add a small egress policy to allow TCP 443 to that service/endpoint (varies by distro).
- Network plugin: these NetworkPolicies require a CNI that implements Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.). If you’re using a basic CNI without policy support, enforcement won’t occur.
- Verify what’s applied:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl get rolebindings -A | egrep 'dev-|staging|prod'
  - kubectl get resourcequota -A
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -A
- Developer ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes v1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa --duration=24h
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa --duration=24h
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa --duration=24h

Want me to:
- switch own-namespace RoleBindings from admin to edit for stricter least privilege?
- enable controlled internet egress for any namespace(s)?
- add an explicit allow to the in-cluster Kubernetes API?

Done.

What I created
- Headless Service statefulset-test/db (for stable network IDs)
- StatefulSet statefulset-test/db with:
  - replicas: 3
  - container: busybox:1.36
  - volumeClaimTemplates: 1Gi RWO PVC per pod, mounted at /data

  2) Attach a new PVC-backed data disk, migrate data as needed, then snapshot.

- Create a DataVolume (need: image/source URL or existing PVC name, desired size, StorageClass).
- Update the VM to use that disk.
- Then create the snapshot named test-snapshot with:

  kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot

    namespace: vm-test-snapshot
  spec:
    source:
      apiGroup: kubevirt.io
      kind: VirtualMachine
      name: snapshot-test-vm

Please tell me:
- Do you want the root disk switched to a DataVolume?

Here’s what I did and found for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init volume referenced a non-existent Secret “vm-cloud-init,” causing the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the cloud-init volume and preventing the VM from starting.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot events: “MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ‘cloudinit-udata’: secret ‘vm-cloud-init’ not found.”

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with basic userData.
- Restarted the VM to re-create the VMI with the now-present cloud-init Secret.

Outcome and verification
- After the fix and restart, vm-troubleshoot shows:
  - The virt-launcher pod was created and successfully scheduled.
  - Containers (guest-console-log, container-disk-binary, volumecontainerdisk-init, compute) were pulled/created/started successfully.
  - No more FailedMount warnings for the cloud-init volume.
- Current VM status is “Starting” with the VMI scheduled and initializing. It has progressed past the previous mount failure and is booting normally. It may take a short time before the VM reports Ready.

If you want, I can keep watching until the VM reaches Ready/RUNNING, or open the console to confirm the guest has fully booted.

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Here’s what I did and found for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init volume referenced a non-existent Secret “vm-cloud-init,” causing the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the cloud-init volume and preventing the VM from starting.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot events: “MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ‘cloudinit-udata’: secret ‘vm-cloud-init’ not found.”

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with basic userData.
- Restarted the VM to re-create the VMI with the now-present cloud-init Secret.

Outcome and verification
- After the fix and restart, vm-troubleshoot shows:
  - The virt-launcher pod was created and successfully scheduled.
  - Containers (guest-console-log, container-disk-binary, volumecontainerdisk-init, compute) were pulled/created/started successfully.
  - No more FailedMount warnings for the cloud-init volume.
- Current VM status is “Starting” with the VMI scheduled and initializing. It has progressed past the previous mount failure and is booting normally. It may take a short time before the VM reports Ready.

If you want, I can keep watching until the VM reaches Ready/RUNNING, or open the console to confirm the guest has fully booted.

Here’s what I did and found for vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init volume referenced a non-existent Secret “vm-cloud-init,” causing the virt-launcher pod to fail mounting the cloud-init volume and preventing the VM from starting.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot events: “MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ‘cloudinit-udata’: secret ‘vm-cloud-init’ not found.”

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with basic userData.
- Restarted the VM to re-create the VMI with the now-present cloud-init Secret.

Outcome and verification
- After the fix and restart, vm-troubleshoot shows:
  - The virt-launcher pod was created and successfully scheduled.
  - Containers (guest-console-log, container-disk-binary, volumecontainerdisk-init, compute) were pulled/created/started successfully.
  - No more FailedMount warnings for the cloud-init volume.
- Current VM status is “Starting” with the VMI scheduled and initializing. It has progressed past the previous mount failure and is booting normally. It may take a short time before the VM reports Ready.

If you want, I can keep watching until the VM reaches Ready/RUNNING, or open the console to confirm the guest has fully booted.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData tells the guest OS to halt immediately after boot. With runStrategy=Always, KubeVirt restarts the VM each time it shuts down, creating a crashloop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In userData runcmd: "shutdown -h now"

How to fix
- If you want the VM to stay up: remove the "shutdown -h now" line from the cloud-init userData and restart the VM so it boots normally.
- If you intended a one-time shutdown and don’t want it auto-restarted: change the VM’s runStrategy from Always to Manual (or Halted), or use RerunOnFailure so a clean shutdown isn’t restarted.
- After updating the spec, stop and start (or restart) the VM so the new cloud-init takes effect.

Steps.message: Waiting for VM to attempt boot and crash...

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData tells the guest OS to halt immediately after boot. With runStrategy=Always, KubeVirt restarts the VM each time it shuts down, creating a crashloop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In userData runcmd: "shutdown -h now"

How to fix
- If you want the VM to stay up: remove the "shutdown -h now" line from the cloud-init userData and restart the VM so it boots normally.
- If you intended a one-time shutdown and don’t want it auto-restarted: change the VM’s runStrategy from Always to Manual (or Halted), or use RerunOnFailure so a clean shutdown isn’t restarted.
- After updating the spec, stop and start (or restart) the VM so the new cloud-init takes effect.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData tells the guest OS to halt immediately after boot. With runStrategy=Always, KubeVirt restarts the VM each time it shuts down, creating a crashloop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In userData runcmd: "shutdown -h now"

I attempted to retrieve guest agent data from test-vm-with-agent in vm-test-guest-info, but the QEMU guest agent is not responding yet.

What I found:
- Guest agent subresource calls failed (cluster reported the VMI guest-agent subresource as unavailable), and the VMI status shows guestOSInfo: {}.
- The VM itself is Running and Ready, but no guest-agent data has been reported yet (common while cloud-init is finishing or before the qemu-guest-agent service starts).

What the guest agent data typically includes (once available):
- OS information:
  - pretty_name (e.g., Fedora 40), version_id, kernel_release (e.g., 6.8.x), architecture, hostname, timezone, boot time/uptime
- Filesystems:
  - For each mounted filesystem: device (e.g., /dev/vda1), mountpoint (/), type (xfs/ext4), total_bytes, used_bytes, free_bytes
- Network interfaces:
  - For each interface: name (e.g., eth0), MAC address, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, link state, MTU
- Logged-in users:
  - For each session: username, tty/console, source/remote host, login time

If you’d like, I can retry in a bit or watch for the guest agent to come up and return the full OS, filesystem, network, and user details as soon as they’re available. If this persists, verify inside the VM that qemu-guest-agent is installed and the service is running/enabled. For Fedora:
- sudo systemctl status qemu-guest-agent
- If not installed: sudo dnf install -y qemu-guest-agent
- Then: sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
